report.summary: Incident S08 is inconclusive: payment-service error rate stepped from about 0.2% to about 21% at 11:00 UTC and stayed near 20-24% through 11:30, while checkout-service 500 warnings began at 11:00:14Z. The only change in the window is payment-service deploy v3.2.0 at 10:57Z, about 3 minutes before onset, which adds idempotency_key writes and an ORM 5.x to 6.x upgrade. Payment-service's own error logs could not be retrieved because every query timed out, and payment-provider has no telemetry, so the failing path is unverified. The system's determination is inconclusive because the leading hypothesis (H1, confidence 0.60) does not meet the criteria, with contradicting evidence at 44% of weighted evidence against a 35% maximum. The deploy is the leading candidate but no cause is asserted; the schema migration status is unknown and checkout's ~9% versus payment-service's ~21% error rate is unexplained.

ranked_hypotheses.mechanism: Deploy v3.2.0 at 10:57Z added idempotency_key writes and an ORM 5.x to 6.x upgrade on the payments write path, so writes fail and payment-service returns 500s from about 11:00, which checkout then propagates as its own 500 warnings. Shallow SELECT 1 and /health checks would not detect a write-path fault.

Payment-service log data that could confirm the exception type remains unavailable

ranked_hypotheses.mechanism: The v3.2.0 schema migration adding the idempotency_key column was run separately and may not have been applied, so inserts that reference the column fail with SQL errors and return 500, matching the P02 pattern. This is a specific sub-case of H1 with the migration as the fault.
assumptions: The migration was not applied before traffic reached the new build
A missing column produces 500s rather than being silently tolerated

ranked_hypotheses.mechanism: A failure in calls from payment-service to the external payment provider begins at about 11:00 and surfaces as payment-service 500s to checkout, with no payments-db or deploy change needed to explain it. Its status-page check was taken after onset and does not show partial call failures.
assumptions: Provider failures are partial and not visible on the status page
Provider telemetry being absent does not mean the provider is healthy

inferred_conclusions.statement: The error step at about 11:00 is a discrete event, not a capacity or load problem, since resource and traffic metrics were flat.

Payment-service deploy v3.2.0 (C09) is the leading candidate for the onset, with a write-path regression as the most likely mechanism, but this is not confirmed because payment-service error logs are unavailable.
A missing idempotency_key column from an unapplied migration is a possible sub-mechanism of the deploy regression, but migration status is unknown.
A payment-provider call failure starting at 11:00 cannot be excluded, because the provider has no telemetry and its status-page check was taken after onset.
payments-db is unlikely to be the origin, because its aggregate metrics and logs show no failure at 11:00, although aggregate metrics would not reveal a specific write error.
Checkout-service is probably a downstream victim of payment-service errors rather than the origin, since its 500 warnings begin after payment-service's error step.

remediation.action: Make schema migrations a gated step of deploys, so code is not released ahead of its migration.

remediation.action: Extend health checks and alerting to cover payment write success and provider call success, not only HTTP status and SELECT 1.
remediation.rationale: Telemetry gaps and shallow checks delayed diagnosis of this incident.

brief.title: payment-service errors
brief.alert: ALERT [P1] payment-service error rate 22% since ~11:00 UTC; payments failing.

plan.incident_understanding: payment-service error rate rose to about 22% since roughly 11:00 UTC, with checkout-service also alerting, so payment failures are propagating upstream into checkout. Telemetry covers 10:00 to 11:30 UTC; change history covers a longer window.
candidate_explanations: A deployment or config change to payment-service around 11:00 UTC introduced a regression causing errors
A failing downstream dependency of payment-service (e.g. payment provider or database) is returning errors or timeouts
A feature flag or infrastructure event (capacity, network, certificate) affected payment-service or its dependencies
A recurrence of a past incident pattern documented in postmortems

tasks.objective: Characterise the error signatures in payment-service and checkout-service logs and the error-rate metric from 10:00 to 11:30 UTC: identify the exact onset time, dominant error types/status codes, and which downstream calls fail most (e.g. timeouts vs 5xx vs auth failures).

List all deployments, config changes, feature flag changes and infra events for payment-service and its direct upstream/downstream dependencies in the 6 hours before 11:30 UTC, highlighting any change close to 11:00 UTC.

Map payment-service's dependency graph and check health of each downstream dependency (databases, payment provider integrations, queues) during 10:30 to 11:30 UTC to determine whether a dependency is the source of the failures; also search past postmortems for similar payment-service error-rate incidents.

Characterise the error signatures in payment-service and checkout-service logs and the error-rate metric from 10:00 to 11:30 UTC: identify the exact onset time, dominant error types/status codes, and which downstream calls fail most (e.g. timeouts vs 5xx vs auth failures).

findings.summary: payment-service error rate jumped from a baseline of about 0.2% (10:00–10:55) to 21.3% in the 11:00 bucket, peaking at 23.6% at 11:10 and ending at 20.6% at 11:30. checkout-service error rate rose from about 0.3% to 9.6% at 11:00 and sat near 8.4–9.6% through 11:30. The checkout logs show the dominant downstream failure is HTTP 500 Internal Server Error from payment-service. Payment-service's own logs could not be retrieved (timeouts), so the server-side cause is unverified. Payment-service CPU, memory, latency and request rate stayed flat across the onset, which argues against resource exhaustion or load as the trigger.

observations.statement: payment-service error_rate was 0.15–0.26% in every 5-minute bucket from 10:00 to 10:55, then 21.26% at 11:00, 22.55% at 11:05, 23.55% at 11:10, 23.28% at 11:15, 21.73% at 11:20, 21.15% at 11:25 and 20.61% at 11:30. The onset is between 10:55 and 11:00.

checkout-service error_rate was 0.25–0.35% in every bucket from 10:00 to 10:55, then 9.61% at 11:00, 8.37% at 11:05, 9.33% at 11:10, 8.44% at 11:15, 8.84% at 11:20, 8.66% at 11:25 and 9.35% at 11:30. Its onset is also at 11:00, the same bucket as payment-service.

Checkout-service WARN/ERROR logs from 10:00 to 11:30 contain 27 lines: 26 WARN and 1 ERROR. 25 of the lines are 'payment-service returned 500 Internal Server Error for order #'. The first of these is at 11:00:14Z (L0182) and they continue at a steady cadence through 11:30:00Z (L0333).
Checkout logs show one retry of an idempotent call to payment-service (attempt 2) at 10:29:28Z, before the 11:00 onset. This is an isolated event and is not part of the error burst.

Checkout logs show one ERROR, 'order b044293f rejected: card declined by issuer' at 11:05:54Z (L0212). This is a card-issuer decline, not a payment-service technical failure, and it is the only non-500 failure signature.
Payment-service CPU stayed at 31.7–32.5% and memory at 53.7–57.1% across 10:55–11:15. Latency p99 stayed at 437–465 ms and request_rate at 57.8–62.2 req/s. None of these shows a step change at 11:00.

Payment-service's own log query timed out on all attempts, both for the full 10:00–11:30 window at WARN level and for the narrower 10:55–11:10 window at ERROR level. No payment-service log lines were obtained, so the exception types, status codes and downstream calls made by payment-service are not known.

interpretations.statement: The failing calls are payment-service returning HTTP 500 to checkout. Checkout's logs show 500s, not timeouts or auth failures, so the dominant error type is 5xx from payment-service.

The failure onset at 11:00 is a step change, not a gradual ramp. Error rate was flat at baseline before 11:00 and near its plateau from the first bucket after. The cause is most likely a discrete change or event just before 11:00 UTC, which the change history should be checked for.

Resource saturation (CPU, memory), a traffic surge and latency degradation in payment-service do not appear to be the trigger. These metrics were flat across the onset, and the error burst is a sharp step, not a degradation curve.

Checkout's error rate (~9%) is roughly half of payment-service's (~21%). This is consistent with only some checkout calls reaching payment-service, or with checkout retries masking some failures, but the data here does not confirm which.

data_gaps: payment-service log queries timed out on all 3 attempts for both the broad window (10:00–11:30, WARN) and the narrow window (10:55–11:10, ERROR). The server-side error signatures, exception types and downstream call failures (timeouts vs 5xx vs auth) for payment-service are therefore unknown.
Checkout logs were only the WARN/ERROR lines (27 total, capped at 50), so INFO-level context around the onset is missing.

Only the 11:00 onset is confirmed. Its exact start within the 10:55–11:00 interval is not resolvable from the 5-minute metric buckets.
suggested_followups: Retry payment-service logs with a much narrower window (e.g. 11:00–11:02) and a specific message filter, or check the log backend's health, to get the exception types and downstream call failures.
Pull change and deploy history for payment-service and its dependencies between 10:45 and 11:00 UTC.
Query payment-service's downstream dependency metrics and error rates (e.g. the card-issuer or database connections) to see which call started failing at 11:00.
Confirm whether the checkout 500s are retried, and compare checkout's failed-order count with payment-service's error count to explain the 9% vs 21% gap.

The closest past incident (P02) is a deploy that shipped before its schema migration, which is a strong hypothesis to test.

critique.summary: H1 (deploy C09 causing write-path 500s) is the best-supported origin: the step at 11:00 follows the 10:57 deploy, and checkout's 500s are downstream. However, the mechanism is untested because payment-service logs were never retrieved, and the analysis mislabels flat resource metrics as contradicting evidence. Payment-provider and payments-db are not cleared by shallow health checks, and the schema migration status is unknown, so H1 and H2 need targeted checks before the conclusion is accepted.

issues.detail: M32, M34, M35 and M36 (flat CPU, latency, memory and request rate) are listed as contradicting H1. They do not contradict a deploy-triggered write-path fault; they only rule out resource saturation and load as the trigger.

A payment-provider call failure surfacing as payment-service 500s fits the same step-change onset and is not ruled out. The only evidence against it is a status-page check taken at 11:28, after onset, which would not show a failure limited to some calls.

The 0.70 confidence rests on the timing of C09 and the plausibility of its content. No ledger record shows a write-path error, an ORM error, or an idempotency_key failure. Payment-service logs were never obtained, and the migration status is unknown, so the write-path mechanism is inferred rather than observed.
P02 is cited as support, but it is a past incident. It shows a similar pattern, not that this incident has the same cause.
H2 (migration not applied) is stated at 0.50, yet the migration status is unknown and no ledger record shows it. It is also a sub-case of H1, so its confidence is not consistent with H1's 0.70.
H12 (SELECT 1 health check of payments-db) is cited as contradicting H2. A shallow connectivity check does not show whether the table schema is complete, so it does not contradict a missing column.

The payments-db analysis cites P07 as a similar pattern, but the P07 root cause was a batch-job connection leak. Nothing in the window shows connection or pool metrics, so H3 is weakly grounded in P07 alone.

Checkout's error rate (~9%) is roughly half of payment-service's (~21%), which is unexplained. If checkout's only failing dependency is payment-service, the rates should be closer. This may point to partial routing or a second failing path, and the analysis does not address it.

analysis.response_to_critique: Misread evidence: flat CPU, latency, memory and request rate are no longer listed as contradicting H1; they only rule out saturation and load as the trigger. Alternative not ruled out: payment-provider failure is now a ranked hypothesis (H3) at 0.2, since the status-page check was post-onset and shallow. Overconfidence: H1 confidence is lowered to 0.6 because no ledger record shows a write-path or ORM error and payment-service logs were never obtained. Unsupported claim: P02 is retained only as a similar pattern, not as proof. Overconfidence on H2: lowered to 0.35 and framed as a sub-case of H1. Misread evidence on H2: H12 is removed from contradicting evidence because a SELECT 1 check does not show schema completeness. Ignored contradiction on payments-db: H3 from the earlier analysis is dropped as a ranked hypothesis because it rests only on P07, a batch-job leak with no supporting metrics in this window. Checkout's lower rate is acknowledged as unexplained and listed as a limitation rather than resolved.

critique.summary: The leading hypothesis (H1, v3.2.0 write-path regression) fits the timing and the checkout 500 pattern, but its mechanism is unverified because payment-service logs were never retrieved and the migration status is unknown. The provider alternative (H3) is dismissed on weak grounds: its only contradiction is the deploy timing, and its missing telemetry is treated as reassurance. Confidence and the framing of supporting evidence should be tightened. No further investigation budget remains, so the report should be revised rather than investigated further.

issues.detail: The payment-provider failure (H3) is not excluded by the evidence. Provider telemetry is entirely absent, and the status-page check ran after onset and is shallow. The deploy at 10:57Z is only a timing coincidence 3 minutes before onset, which is the classic trap of blaming a change because it happened near onset. Nothing in the ledger shows that the 500s originate in the DB write path rather than in provider calls.

Confidence 0.60 is high for a mechanism whose exception type, endpoint and downstream call were never observed. The payment-service error logs timed out on every attempt, so the write-path cause rests on the change description and inference, not on error signatures.

H12 (payments-db SELECT 1 healthy) is listed as supporting H1, but a green SELECT 1 neither supports nor contradicts a payment-service write-path fault. It only shows the check cannot detect the fault. It should be treated as neutral.

H2 is a sub-case of H1 (the same change, with the migration as the fault) and is presented as a separate hypothesis. This double-counts the same evidence. Its 0.35 confidence and the H1 0.60 are not independent. Migration status is unknown, so H2 should be merged into H1 as a sub-mechanism.

H3 is contradicted by C09 only on timing. A recent deploy does not refute a provider failure beginning at the same time, so the contradiction is weak and should not drive the low confidence on its own. The 0.20 confidence should rest on the lack of provider evidence, not on C09.

The checkout 9% versus payment-service 21% gap is unexplained and could indicate partial routing or retries masking failures. The report should state that this gap weakens the claim that payment-service is the sole origin, rather than leaving it as an open note.
